notes.heading: A small function value can hide a rapidly changing slope
paragraphs: Continuity and differentiability are local properties with different requirements. A function can approach its value while its slopes oscillate or grow without a finite limit. To test a derivative at a special point, use the function's actual value there in the difference quotient; a formula valid only away from the point may be insufficient. Bounding the quotient can establish convergence even when oscillation prevents direct substitution. After a derivative has been established at one point, do not infer that nearby derivative values converge to it.

questions.prompt: Define f(0)=0 and f(x)=x²sin(1/x) for x≠0. Use the definition and |sin t|≤1 to find f′(0).
solution: For h≠0 the quotient is h sin(1/h).
Its absolute value is at most |h|, which tends to zero.

questions.prompt: For f(0)=0 and f(x)=x²sin(1/x) away from zero, it is known that f′(0)=0. For x≠0, f′(x)=2x sin(1/x)-cos(1/x). Does f′ approach 0 as x→0?
questions.answer: No. At x_n=1/(2πn), f′(x_n)=-1, while at y_n=1/((2n+1)π), f′(y_n)=1.
solution: Both positive sequences approach zero as n increases.
Evaluate the sine and cosine terms to obtain two distinct limiting values.
markingPoints: Give two sequences tending to zero.
Conclude that the derivative is not continuous at zero.

questions.prompt: The function f(x)=√x is defined only for x≥0. Explain why the usual two-sided real derivative at 0 is unavailable, and examine the right difference quotient.
questions.answer: There are no domain values to the left. The right quotient is 1/√h for h>0 and grows without bound, so there is no finite right derivative either.
solution: State the domain restriction for a two-sided limit.
Simplify √h/h and examine h→0 from the right.
markingPoints: State the absence of a finite right derivative.
